sections.title_en: The Lord's Conduct of the World Through Nature, and the Value of the Wonder
sections.body_en:
As we have learned at length (chapter 18), the ordinary conduct of the world is through the ways of nature. That is, the Lord created the world with wisdom and conducts it according to the laws embedded in it, so that a person can understand the result of his actions. If he chooses good, he will add good, and if he chooses evil, he will add evil. And although one cannot foresee with certainty what will be, since within the framework of the laws of nature there are many factors that influence every event, nevertheless one can generally estimate what will probably be. For example, one can estimate that if a person ploughs and sows his field before the winter, when the winter comes rain will fall, and in the spring he will merit to reap his grain. Admittedly, sometimes the rains are withheld, or a blight attacks his field, or a robber seizes his land, or an enemy conquers his country, and then he will not merit to reap his grain. Therefore it is not enough for a person to be diligent in working his field; rather, for greater security he must also store some of his grain for the coming years, lest the rains not fall or a blight attack his field. And he must organise himself within a communal and national framework, so that there will be police to protect his land from robbers and an army to protect his country from enemies.

Life within this framework of the laws of nature enables a person to reveal the image of God within him, to develop all his talents, and to draw the word of the Lord into the world in such a way that the laws of nature do not limit him but, on the contrary, intensify his powers. On the other hand, however, the difficulty of surviving within the framework of the laws of nature may cause a person to forget his faith and his destiny, until he accepts reality as a fact that cannot be changed, compromising with all the injustices within it. For example, he will be willing to enslave himself to the rich in order to insure himself against drought or blight in his field, and he will crown tyrannical rulers over himself in order to defend himself against robbers and enemies, and he will despair of changing his situation. Until it seems that darkness covers the earth and the laws of nature imprison man, and in order to survive he is forced to give up his faith and his values.

Like stars shining in the darkness, the wonder-workers, who cleave to the Lord and to the values of truth and goodness without compromise, fan the fire of faith in people's hearts and remind them that the Lord conducts the world, that the laws of nature are subject to Him, and that He loves the righteous and answers their prayers, and at times performs for them wonders that break through the limits of nature. Their conduct suits exceptional individuals who are scrupulous in mitzvot over and beyond what is required by the guidance of the Torah, while overcoming their nature enormously, and they thereby connect to a supreme level beyond this world. To the level that we will reach in the future, when the Lord's providence over all His creatures will be revealed, and the righteous will be rewarded and the wicked will be punished. Admittedly, the wonders are performed only rarely, so as not to harm the order of nature that is necessary for the repair of the world; yet through their wondrous lives, the wonder-workers give the ordinary person inspiration to believe that if he strengthens himself in Torah and mitzvot, he will merit to be freed from enslavement to the shackles that prevent him from repairing himself. They also give inspiration to the great Torah scholars to uncover the hidden things within the framework of the laws of nature, so that they can guide the public in the ways of the Lord, in such a way that the laws of nature will help them continue to advance toward the repair of the world and its redemption.

However, since the way of the world is that it is conducted according to nature, and the miracle is meant to reveal the Lord's will in the world and not to change its order, the wonder-workers strive to cleave to the trait of humility and not to benefit from the miracle. And when they were not careful about this, they suffered afflictions (as explained below in sections 3-6).

sections.title_en: The Great Rabbis and the Wonder-Workers
sections.body_en:
It once happened that Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa went to study Torah with Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, and the son of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai fell ill. Rabbi Yoḥanan said to him: "Ḥanina my son, pray for mercy for him and he will live." Rabbi Ḥanina placed his head between his knees and prayed for mercy for him – and he recovered. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said: "Had ben Zakkai pressed his head between his knees the entire day, they would have paid no attention to him." Rabbi Yoḥanan's wife said to him: "Is Ḥanina your disciple greater than you?" He said to her: "No, but he is like a servant before the king, and I am like a minister before the king" (Berakhot 34b).

That is, the role of the minister is to understand the will of the king and to be his partner in shaping economic, social, military and judicial policy, in order to benefit the kingdom. And if he attends to private problems, he will neglect his general duties, and perhaps he will even betray his office and use public resources for those close to him. By contrast, the servant does not presume to understand the general policy and does not try to influence it, but out of his admiration for the king and for the importance of his role, he attends to all the king's personal needs with love and loyalty, so that the king can lead the kingdom in the best possible way. Since this is so, he is especially close to the king, and he is able to ask him, on behalf of private individuals, personal requests that suit the king's good-heartedness, provided that they are carried out discreetly, in a way that does not violate the rules by which the kingdom is run.

Similarly, the wonder-workers are righteous people whose souls are bound to Heaven; while working for their livelihood they cleave to truth and goodness, and in their free time they devote themselves modestly and in secret to Torah, to kindness and to prayer. As a result, wonders are performed through them that bring blessing from a supreme level that will be revealed in the future, and that strengthen the faith that the Lord conducts the world. And although they did not teach Torah to the many as the rabbis do, their modest lives are an example and a model of a person's ability to connect through faith to eternal values and to draw rays of light and salvation from the upper world.

By contrast, the great rabbis do not withdraw into personal service of the Lord; rather, out of deep study of the word of the Lord revealed in the Torah, they teach Torah and guide the public to be honest and diligent in their work, to sanctify their lives by keeping Shabbatot and festivals and by being careful about prohibitions, to establish families with joy and love, to thank the Lord with blessings, to settle the Land, and to pray for the redemption. In this way they bring blessing to the world in the finest way, for the main blessing comes to the community and to the individual through Israel understanding their destiny and choosing to fulfil the Torah and the mitzvot. And if they withdraw into personal service of the Lord in the manner of the wonder-workers, they will betray their role, for they are like ministers to the king.

Similarly, the Talmud relates (Ta'anit 21b) that in Sura, the city of the great Amora Rav, a plague spread and many people died of it, but in Rav's neighbourhood the plague did not spread. People thought that this was presumably in the merit of Rav. They were shown in a dream that Rav's merit was greater, and that the fact that the plague did not spread was in the merit of a righteous man who used to lend tools for burying poor dead people. It was further related that in Drokart, the city of the great Amora Rav Huna, a fire broke out, and it did not reach Rav Huna's neighbourhood. People thought that this was presumably in the merit of Rav Huna, but they were shown in a dream that Rav Huna's merit was greater, and that the rescue from the fire was in the merit of a righteous woman who used to heat her oven every Friday and let all the poor women cook their dishes in her oven.

sections.title_en: One Should Not Benefit from Miracles
sections.body_en:
The miracle is meant to reveal the will of the Lord but not to change the order of the world; therefore, one who seeks to benefit from a miracle violates the will of the Lord, and may thereby cause the public to sin by thinking that one can rely on miracles, contrary to the will of the Lord that a person should strive to sustain himself through the ways of nature (see above 18:11). Therefore, the Sages warned not to benefit from a miracle, and "the more one can distance oneself from miraculous acts, the better and more proper it is" (Rashi, Ta'anit 24b). And although the wonder-workers know that using a miracle is dangerous, at times the evil inclination may overpower them and entice them to make a little use of a miracle for their own needs, such as when they are in very straitened circumstances, or when the inclination to pride slightly bends their judgement into thinking that there is a sanctification of God's name in it. And when they stumble in this even slightly, they arouse great accusations and bring harsh afflictions upon themselves (see below sections 5-6). Therefore, the Sages said (Shabbat 32a) that a person, even if he is righteous, may not rely on a miracle, lest a miracle not be performed for him. And even if a miracle is performed for him, it is deducted from his merits. Therefore, righteous people for whom a miracle was performed were careful not to benefit from it.

It is likewise related (Ta'anit 24a) about Elazar of Birta that he would give every bit of money he earned to the charity collectors, to the point that when the charity collectors saw him, they would hide from him, so that he would not give them all his money without leaving anything for himself. One day Elazar went to the market to buy what was needed for his daughter's dowry for her wedding. The charity collectors saw him and hid from him. He ran after them and made them swear to tell him for what charity they were collecting. They said to him: We are collecting money for the wedding of an orphan boy and an orphan girl. He swore and said: They take precedence over my daughter! He gave them all the money he had set aside for his daughter's dowry. He was left with one zuz, and with it he bought a little wheat and put it in the storehouse. His wife asked her daughter, the bride: Did you see what your father brought? She said: Whatever he brought, he put in the storehouse. His wife went to open the storehouse and could not open it because of the abundance of wheat that filled all of it. His daughter went to the study hall and said to him: "Come and see what the One who loves you has done for you." He understood that a miracle had been performed for him, swore and said: They are hereby consecrated to the poor, and you shall have no more of this wheat than any other poor person. All this was because he did not want to benefit from the miracle.1

Similarly, it is related (Ta'anit 24b) about the great Amora Rava that he ruled in his court that a man who had committed adultery with a gentile woman be punished with lashes. Unintentionally, the adulterer died from the lashes. The Persian king wanted to punish Rava, since the Jews had not been granted authority to impose the death penalty. His mother, Ifra Hormiz, said to him: Do not get involved with the Jews, for whatever they ask of the Lord, He answers them, and even when they pray for rain He answers them. The king said to his mother: To see whether your words are true, ask Rava to pray now, in the summer, that rain should fall. Ifra Hormiz sent a request to Rava that he pray for rain to fall. He prayed for rain and it did not fall. He prayed again, pleading in distress for rain to fall, and the Lord answered him and much rain fell. At night, Rava's father appeared to him in a dream and wondered how he had dared to ask to change the laws of nature, and he instructed him to change the place where he slept. Rava did so, and in the morning he found that his regular bed had been slashed with knives. Thus he was shown from Heaven that he had deserved punishment, but since he changed his place and understood the danger that comes from using a miracle, he was saved.

Further on this matter, the Sages related (Ta'anit 23b) about Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elyashiv, who was a wonder-worker. His disciple Rabbi Mani said to him: The wealthy members of my father-in-law's family are making me suffer. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: Let them become poor! And they became poor. After a time Rabbi Mani said to him: Now that they are poor, they are pressing me to help them. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: Let them become rich! And they became rich again. Rabbi Mani further said to him: My wife Ḥanna is not beautiful in my eyes. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: Let Ḥanna become beautiful! And she became beautiful. After a time Rabbi Mani said to him: Since she became beautiful, she lords it over me. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: Let Ḥanna return to her plainness! And she returned to her plainness. Afterwards two students came to Rabbi Yitzḥak and asked him to pray for them that they become wise in their studies. He answered them: "It was with me, and I sent it away." That is, I once had the power to bless, but I gave it up, for I came to realise that it is better to accept the Lord's conduct of the world as it is, without trying to change it.

notes_en.en: Likewise in Ta'anit 24b, they ruled that one should not benefit from wheat that arrived in a ship by a miracle. It is further explained in Ta'anit 20b that Rav Huna had wine in a dilapidated building, and he wanted to remove the wine from there before the building collapsed. Rav Huna brought Rav Adda bar Ahava in there and drew out a Torah discussion with him at length until he had finished clearing out the wine. After Rav Adda bar Ahava left, the building collapsed. Rav Adda bar Ahava understood that Rav Huna had used his merits so that the building would not fall, and he was displeased with Rav Huna; "he held in accordance with what Rabbi Yannai said: A person should never stand in a place of danger and say, 'A miracle will be performed for me,' lest a miracle not be performed for him; and if you say that a miracle is performed for him, it is deducted from his merits. Rav Ḥanan said: What is the verse? As it is written (Bereshit 32:11): 'I am diminished by all the kindnesses and by all the truth.'" Similarly, in Kiddushin 29b, Abaye arranged for Rabbi Ya'akov son of Rav Aḥa to sleep in the study hall in which there was a harmful demon, for he estimated that the demon would try to harm the righteous man and would be destroyed as a result of the righteous man's prayer. And so it was. Yet Rabbi Ya'akov was displeased that he had endangered him. See above 18:9, that one does not rely on miracles, and the mitzvot must be fulfilled through the way of nature.

sections.title_en: When It Is Permitted to Benefit from a Miracle
sections.body_en:
As we learned in the previous section, wonder-workers must refrain from using miracles for their own needs, for the miracle is meant to reveal the greatness of the Lord and to show that the world can be changed through faith and Torah, and not to be made use of. And one who uses a miracle for his personal needs is like a kohen who uses the sacred things of the Temple for his personal needs, who commits me'ila (misuse of consecrated property) and thereby endangers his life.

But when a wonder-worker helps simple and innocent people through a miracle, they are permitted to benefit from it. This is like the way Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa blessed his neighbour: it turned out that the beams she had bought for the roof of her house were too short, and he ordered them to lengthen, and they lengthened (Ta'anit 25a). And there is no misuse of sacred things of Heaven in this use, since through the wonder the greatness of the Lord, who loves the righteous and takes their request into account, was revealed (Gevurat Ari there). Nor is there concern that they will learn to rely on miracles, since innocent people do not presume to think that from now on the Lord will sustain them through miracles; rather, they see the miracle as a one-time gift that expresses the Lord's love for the righteous and for them, and they are encouraged by it in their work. But when the miracle is performed for a learned person, he may become proud, or become lax in the effort to repair the world through the ways of nature by means of Torah, mitzvot and good deeds.

Similarly, the Sages said (Shabbat 53b): "It once happened that a man's wife died and left a son to be nursed, and he did not have the wages of a wet nurse to give, and a miracle was performed for him and he developed breasts like a woman's two breasts and he nursed his son. Rav Yosef said: Come and see how great this man is, that such a miracle was performed for him! Abaye said to him: On the contrary, how inferior this man is, that the order of creation was changed for him!" One can explain that if he was a simple person, one should be impressed by his greatness, that a miracle was performed for him. But if he was learned, the matter testifies to his being inferior, in that he needed such a miracle. The Sages concluded and said: See how it is easier to perform a miracle for a man so that he can nurse than to create a livelihood for him. That is, it is harder to change the laws of the economic market than to change the body of one person contrary to nature.

When the miracle occurs in a natural way to a person not known as a wonder-worker, it is permitted to benefit from it, for since there is a logical explanation of how it came about, it does not change the order of nature. As the Sages said (Shabbat 150b): "It once happened that a breach opened in the field of a certain pious man, and he considered fencing it, and he remembered that it was Shabbat, and that pious man refrained and did not fence it (even on a weekday, since he regarded it as a sin on his part that he had thought about it on Shabbat). And a miracle was performed for him and a caper bush grew in it (a thorny fruit bush that fenced his field), and from it came his livelihood and the livelihood of the members of his household."

Likewise, when a person performs a mitzva and is blessed in its merit, this is not a miracle that is not in the way of nature, but rather a divine blessing that comes through the ways of nature. As the Sages said (Ta'anit 9a) that one who gives tithes becomes rich, as it is said (Devarim 14:22): "'You shall surely tithe' (aser te'aser) – tithe so that you will become rich (titasher)." And so Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi explained that the wealthy of the Land of Israel became wealthy because they separated tithes (Shabbat 119a). And it was likewise related (Megilla 27b) about the grandmother of Rabbi Zakkai that she sold her head-covering in order to buy wine for Kiddush, and she and her descendants merited great wealth. And it was likewise related (there) about Rav Huna that he pawned his belt in order to buy wine for Kiddush, and in this merit his teacher Rav blessed him, and he became so rich that all the women of his family were dressed in costly silk garments.

Wonder-workers cleave to a higher world, in which the demands are stricter. By virtue of this they are at times able to bring about wonders that are not in the way of nature, but as a result of this attachment it is hard for them to reconcile themselves to the compromises required in this world, and therefore they suffer afflictions.

The Sages said (Ta'anit 21a) about Naḥum Ish Gamzu, who was accustomed to miracles, that they called him "Ish Gamzu" because he used to say about everything that happened to him: "This too is for the good (gam zu le-tova)." When the Sages needed to send a gift to the emperor so that he would be favourably disposed toward the Jews, they sent Naḥum Ish Gamzu, since he was accustomed to miracles. They placed in his hands a chest full of precious stones and pearls. On his way he lodged at an inn, and at night the innkeepers stole the stones and pearls from the chest and put earth in their place. He said, "This too is for the good," and brought the chest to the king. When the king saw that the chest was full of earth, he became angry and wanted to kill the Jews. Eliyahu the prophet came disguised as one of the ministers and said to the king: Perhaps this is some of the earth of Avraham their father, which would turn into swords when he threw it at his enemies. There was a province that the king had been unable to conquer; he made use of the earth and conquered it. They filled Naḥum Ish Gamzu's chest with precious stones and pearls and sent him off with great honour. When the innkeepers heard that their earth had turned into swords, they brought more earth to the king and said that this was the earth that had turned into swords, but when they tested their earth, they saw that it remained as it was, and they killed them for their attempt to deceive the king.

Together with being accustomed to miracles, he was beset with harsh afflictions (Ta'anit 21a): "They said about Naḥum Ish Gam Zu that he was blind in both eyes, his two hands were amputated, his two legs were amputated, and his whole body was covered with boils, and he was lying in a dilapidated house, and the legs of his bed were placed in bowls of water so that ants would not climb onto him… (since the house was about to collapse) his disciples wanted to remove his bed and afterwards remove the vessels. He said to them: My sons, remove the vessels and afterwards remove my bed, for you are assured that as long as I am in the house, the house will not fall. They removed the vessels and afterwards removed his bed, and the house fell. His disciples said to him: Rabbi, since you are a completely righteous man, why has this befallen you? He said to them: My sons, I brought it upon myself. For once I was travelling on the road to my father-in-law's house, and I had with me a load on three donkeys, one of food, one of drink and one of various delicacies. A poor man came and stood in my way and said to me: Rabbi, sustain me! I said to him: Wait until I unload the donkey. I had not managed to unload the donkey before his soul departed. I went and fell on my face and said: My eyes that had no pity on your eyes – let them become blind; my hands that had no pity on your hands – let them be amputated; my legs that had no pity on your legs – let them be amputated. And my mind was not at ease until I said: Let my whole body be covered with boils. They said to him: Woe to us that we have seen you thus! He said to them: Woe to me if you had not seen me thus."

Had this incident happened to other rabbis, they would have been very sorry about the poor man's death, but they would not have considered it a grave sin, since they had intended to feed the poor man. Even if another person had told Naḥum Ish Gamzu that this had happened to him, he would presumably have judged him favourably. But being a man of wonders, he made extremely strict demands of himself, to the point that he was compelled to accept terrible afflictions upon himself.

It is likewise related (Ta'anit 24a) about Rabbi Yosi of Yokrat, who was accustomed to miracles. Once he hired workers to work in his field; he was delayed and did not bring them their meal. The workers said to his son: We are hungry. They were sitting under a fig tree; the son said: "Fig tree, fig tree, put forth your fruit so that Father's workers may eat." The fig tree put forth its fruit and the workers ate. Meanwhile Rabbi Yosi arrived and asked their forgiveness for having been delayed, since he had been occupied with a mitzva matter. The workers said to him: "May the Lord satisfy you just as your son satisfied us," and they told him that his son had brought forth figs for them by a miracle. Rabbi Yosi said to his son: "My son, you troubled your Maker to make a fig tree put forth its fruit not in its season – may you be gathered in not in your season." And so it was: his son died. It was further related that he had a "beautiful" daughter; one day he saw a man peeping through the fence at his daughter. He said to him: What are you doing?! The man answered Rabbi Yosi: Since I will not merit to take her as a wife, at least I will merit to gaze at her beauty. Rabbi Yosi said to his daughter: "My daughter, you cause people distress – return to your dust, and let people not stumble through you." And so it was: his daughter died. Here we have a man of wonders bound to the upper world, whose demands are very strict, to the point that he could not consent that his son use his power to solve the problems of the moment, or that his daughter use her power to enhance her beauty, and he held that it was better for them to ascend innocent to the upper world and not be drawn after sin. The Gemara relates that as a result, his disciple, Rabbi Yosi bar Avin, left him and went to study with Rav Ashi, for he feared that he too might incur his displeasure.

The Sages said (Ta'anit 23a): Once, almost the entire winter had passed and no rain had fallen. They sent a request to Ḥoni Ha-me'aggel (the circle-drawer) to pray so that rain would fall. "He prayed and rain did not fall. He drew a circle and stood inside it… He said before Him: Master of the universe, Your children have turned their faces to me, for I am like a member of Your household before You; I swear by Your great name that I will not move from here until You have mercy on Your children! Rain began to drip. His disciples said to him… It seems to us that the rain is falling only to release your oath. He said (to the Holy One, blessed be He): This is not what I asked for, but rather rain for cisterns, ditches and caves. It fell furiously… His disciples said to him… It seems to us that the rain is falling only to destroy the world. He said before Him: This is not what I asked for, but rather rain of goodwill, blessing and generosity. It fell in its proper manner, until all the people went up to the Temple Mount because of the rain. They said to him: Rabbi, just as you prayed that it fall, so pray that it go away. He said to them: This is the tradition I have received, that one does not pray about an excess of good. Nevertheless, bring me a bull of thanksgiving. They brought him a bull of thanksgiving. He placed his two hands on it and said before Him: Master of the universe, Your people Israel whom You brought out of Egypt can bear neither an excess of good nor an excess of punishment. You were angry with them – they could not bear it; You bestowed good upon them – they could not bear it. May it be Your will that the rain stop and there be relief in the world. Immediately the wind blew, the clouds dispersed and the sun shone, and the people went out to the field and brought themselves truffles and mushrooms. Shimon ben Shetaḥ (the Nasi of the Sanhedrin) sent to him: Were you not Ḥoni, I would decree excommunication upon you (for you speak insolently toward Heaven, saying 'This is not what I asked for')… But what can I do to you, for you act petulantly before the Omnipresent and He does your will, like a son who acts petulantly toward his father and he does his will, and he says to him: Father, take me to bathe in hot water, rinse me in cold water, give me nuts, almonds, peaches and pomegranates – and he gives him. And about you the verse says (Mishlei 23:25): 'Let your father and your mother rejoice, and let her who bore you be glad.'" It is possible that Ḥoni Ha-me'aggel felt that he had no choice, and that for the sake of the public he had to pray for rain with insolent words in public; yet his life did not end in the way of all the earth.

The Sages related (Ta'anit 23a) that Ḥoni fell asleep for seventy years, and when he awoke he went to the study hall and told those studying that he was Ḥoni Ha-me'aggel, and they did not believe him. He became so distressed that he prayed for mercy that he might die, and he died. In the book Antiquities of the Jews (14:2), it is related that during the war between the Hasmonean brothers, Yehuda and Aristobulus, the men of Yehuda's faction seized Ḥoni and demanded that he offer a prayer against Aristobulus's faction. But he refused, and prayed to the Lord that He not listen to the prayers of these against those, for they were all members of the Lord's people and His priests. The wicked men surrounded him and killed him by stoning. The Maharsha explained (Ta'anit 23a) that apparently Ḥoni managed to evade them and fell asleep for seventy years, so that everyone was sure that he had been killed by the wicked men; therefore, when he arose after seventy years, even his grandson did not believe him that he was Ḥoni Ha-me'aggel.

Ḥoni's grandsons too were accustomed to miracles, but they lived in poverty and modesty and were spared the afflictions. The Sages related (Ta'anit 23b) about Abba Ḥilkiya, the son of Ḥoni Ha-me'aggel's son, that he was extremely poor, and when the people needed rain, the Sages would ask him to pray and it would fall. Once they sent a pair of Sages to him to ask him to pray for rain. They found him working as a day labourer in a field; they greeted him and he did not return their greeting, nor did he even show them a welcoming face, for he feared that by speaking with them he would neglect his work and thus be stealing from the employer. When he returned home he gathered wood and placed it on one shoulder and his cloak on the other shoulder, for the cloak he had was borrowed and he did not want it to be damaged by the wood. The whole way he walked barefoot, for being extremely poor he did not want to wear out his shoes, and only when he passed through water did he put them on, to protect himself from snakebites. When he reached thorns he lifted his garment, for he feared it would be damaged by the thorns, but he was not concerned about his legs, for even if they were wounded, they would heal afterwards. When he ate at his table he did not offer them to eat with him, for he did not have bread for them. Even in distributing bread to his children he acted very sparingly. Meanwhile, he turned to his wife and said to her in a whisper: I know that these Sages have come to ask about rain; let us go up to the roof and, without their noticing, pray for mercy; perhaps the Holy One, blessed be He, will be appeased and bring down rain, without their thinking that the rain is in the merit of our prayer. They went up and prayed, and the clouds began to come from the side where his wife had prayed, because she used to distribute some of her meagre bread to hungry poor people. When they came down from the roof he said to the messengers: "Blessed is the Omnipresent, who did not make you need Abba Ḥilkiya." But they knew that the rain had fallen in his merit.

They further related (Ta'anit 23b) about Ḥanan Ha-neḥba, the son of Ḥoni Ha-me'aggel's daughter, that when the people needed rain, they would send to him "schoolchildren" to ask him to pray for rain. And the children would grasp the hem of his garment and say to him: "Abba, Abba (Father, Father), give us rain." Ḥanan Ha-neḥba would turn to the Lord and say: "Master of the universe, act for the sake of these who cannot distinguish between the Abba who gives rain and the abba who does not give rain," and rain would fall. And why did they call him Ḥanan Ha-neḥba (the one who hid)? Because he fled from honour and did not want to be appointed to a leading position (Rabbeinu Ḥananel; Arukh), and when they came to ask him to pray for rain, he would hide, so that they would not regard him as accustomed to miracles. Therefore they sent children to him, for they knew that he would not refuse them (Iyun Ya'akov).

The Sages said about Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa (Mishna Berakhot 5:5) that he used to pray for the sick, and after his prayer he could say: This one will live and that one will die. They asked him: How do you know? He said to them: If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, so that it comes out in a flow without hesitation or error – I know that the sick person will recover. And if not – I know that the hour has turned against him and he will not live. They further said (Berakhot 34b): It once happened that the son of Rabban Gamliel fell ill, and he sent two Torah scholars to Rabbi Ḥanina so that he would pray for mercy for him. As soon as he saw them, Rabbi Ḥanina understood that they had come to ask on behalf of Rabban Gamliel's son; he went up to the attic and prayed for mercy for him. When he came down, he said to them: "Go, for the fever has left him," that is, his temperature has dropped and he has begun to recover. They said to him: "Are you a prophet? He said to them: I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but this is the tradition I have received: If my prayer is fluent in my mouth – I know that it is accepted, and if not – I know that it is rejected."

In a certain place there was an arvad (a dangerous venomous reptile) that was harming people. Without his knowing about it, it happened that Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa stood to pray there, and the arvad came out and bit him, and because of his great concentration he did not feel it. After he finished his prayer and left, they found the arvad dead (Yerushalmi Berakhot 5:1). And some say that they told Rabbi Ḥanina about the dangerous arvad, and he went and placed his foot over the arvad's hole; the arvad came out and bit him, and the arvad died. Rabbi Ḥanina took it on his shoulder and brought it to the study hall, and said to them: "See, my sons, it is not the arvad that kills; rather, sin kills. At that time they said: Woe to the person whom an arvad encounters, and woe to the arvad that Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa encounters" (Bavli Berakhot 33a).

Righteous people of the kind of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa are bound with their entire being to supreme levels of truth and piety, and therefore they are not willing to benefit from a peruta that is not clean of any trace of theft or fraud, and therefore their livelihood is often very meagre. And although out of love and compassion they sometimes perform wonders and draw salvation from the upper world for the sake of others, they themselves live in abject poverty. As the Sages said (Ta'anit 24b), that every day of the days of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's righteousness, a heavenly voice would go forth from Heaven and say: "The whole world is sustained for the sake of Ḥanina My son, and Ḥanina My son makes do with a kav of carobs from one Shabbat eve to the next" (see also Berakhot 61b).

However, it was not easy for the family members of these righteous people. The Sages related (Ta'anit 24b) that the wife of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa was very ashamed of her poverty, and so that the neighbours would not sense that she had no ḥallot and cooked dishes for Shabbat, every Friday she would burn in her oven a material that gives off smoke. She had a wicked neighbour who said to herself: She is poor and has no ḥallot and cooked dishes for Shabbat; I will go in to see where the smoke is coming from. She knocked on the door of her house; Rabbi Ḥanina's wife was ashamed and went into the inner room to hide. The neighbour entered the house, and a miracle occurred and she saw the oven full of ḥallot and the kneading vessels full of dough. She called to Rabbi Ḥanina's wife: Bring a baker's shovel to take the ḥallot out of the oven before they burn.

Later, when the suffering of her poverty grew severe, she said to Rabbi Ḥanina: How long will we continue to suffer so much? He said to her: What shall we do? She said to him: Pray for mercy from the Lord that He give us something. He prayed for mercy, and something like the palm of a hand came down, and in it a table leg of gold. At night they dreamt that in the future all the righteous would sit in the World to Come at a golden table with three legs, and they would be at a table with two legs. His wife said to him: Is it good for us that it should be so? He said to her: What shall we do? She said to him: Pray for mercy that they take the golden leg back from us. He prayed for mercy and they took it. They said (Mishna Sota 9:15): "When Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa died, the men of deeds ceased," those who support themselves from their work (Etz Yosef) and do wondrous deeds (Bartenura). Rabbi Yoḥanan related a wondrous thing: Once we were sailing at sea and we saw a chest containing precious stones and pearls, and around it sharks were swimming to guard it. An amudai (diver) wanted to take it; the sharks became agitated and tried to bite him; he threw vinegar at the sharks and they fled. A heavenly voice went forth and said: "What have you to do with this chest, which is reserved for the wife of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, who will in the future store tekhelet in it and distribute it to the righteous in the time to come!" (Bava Batra 74a-b).2

notes_en.en: The stories are in my own words, with commentary. Regarding the dream about the golden leg: in our version of the Gemara Rabbi Ḥanina dreamt, while according to Rashi's version his wife dreamt, and therefore I wrote "they dreamt." In Shemot Rabba 52:3 a similar story is brought about Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta, and there his wife did not agree to benefit from the stone that he had received from Heaven. Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa handled other people's money with extra meticulousness, as related in Ta'anit 25a: once a man passed by his house and forgot some hens there. His wife found them, and Rabbi Ḥanina said to her: Do not eat their eggs, for they belong to their owners. The hens brooded on the eggs, and chicks hatched from them, which grew and also laid eggs, until they were bothering them. Rabbi Ḥanina sold them and bought goats with the proceeds. Years later a man passed by there and said to his companion: "Here is where I left my hens." Rabbi Ḥanina heard and gave him the goats. About these goats the neighbours once complained that they were damaging their fields. Rabbi Ḥanina was sure that it was impossible that the goats in his possession were causing damage. He said: If the goats are damaging your fields, let bears eat them; and if not, let each of them bring a bear on its horns in the evening. And so it was. (The Sages decreed not to raise goats in the Land of Israel, as brought in Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 13:14; the Gevurat Ari explained that he raised them in a forest, and in such a manner it is permitted.) Thus he could have earned a respectable living, but apparently he feared any hint of a monetary transgression, and therefore his livelihood was hard, like what is related about Abba Ḥilkiya (above, section 6). They further said (Ta'anit 25a) that one Friday night he saw that his daughter was sad. He asked: What happened? She answered: By mistake I put vinegar in the Shabbat lamp instead of oil. He said to her: "Why do you care? He who told the oil to burn will tell the vinegar to burn." The lamp burned until the end of Shabbat, and they took fire from it for the Havdala candle. This level belongs to the upper world, in which the substances are united (see Ben Yehoyada, Ta'anit there). It was further said about him in Kohelet Rabba 1:1 that angels helped him raise a stone that he had hewn and beautified for the Temple. In Pesaḥim 112b it is related that from the time of Rabbi Ḥanina's encounter with the demoness Igrat bat Maḥalat, the process of nullifying the influence of demons began (below 26, note 12). And see Yoma 53b and Ḥagiga 14a. (It is worth noting that some commentators tend to interpret the wonders in a way that brings them closer to the way of nature, but the principle that there is still a wonder remains in place.)

sections.title_en: The Prayers and Blessings of Rabbis
sections.body_en:
Generally, the rabbis – the great Torah scholars and the halakhic decisors – did not occupy themselves with wonders; rather, they dedicated their lives to the study of Torah and to teaching it to students and to the wider public, so that they would walk in the ways of the Lord and merit all the good that the Lord promised Israel His people through the ways of nature. As it is said (Devarim 10:12-13): "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways and to love Him, and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul; to keep the commandments of the Lord and His statutes, which I command you this day for your good."

When trouble befell the public, for example when the rains were withheld, they did not seek to be saved through wonders; rather, they established a public fast for repentance and prayer according to the guidance of the Torah, and they would pray at the head of the congregation, and sometimes they were answered, as related about Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva (Ta'anit 25b). And when they were not answered, they saw themselves as rebuked, and sometimes, as a result of their distress at the disgrace of their prayer not being answered, they prayed again in humility and were answered, as happened to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, to Rav Naḥman and to Rav Pappa (Ta'anit 24a-b). Only rarely, when the winter had almost passed and no rain had fallen, did they turn to wonder-workers to pray for them (above, section 6).

Admittedly, at times those who asked the great rabbis for a halakhic ruling or for guidance sensed that there was also in their answers a blessing that was fulfilled in a wondrous way. But the great rabbis took care to avoid thinking that miracles were being performed for them, and they explained the blessing that came in their wake through the ways of nature. For their main role is to teach Torah, whereas wonders are a side matter, which, if importance is attributed to it, may do more harm than good. For we have already learned (above, section 3) that since the miracle violates the order of the world, it arouses accusations and there is danger in it. And most serious of all, it may lead to error, that people will rely on the rabbi's blessing and not exert themselves in Torah, repentance and good deeds. Therefore, even when onlookers from outside sensed that a wondrous power lay hidden in the rabbis' advice and blessing, the rabbis explained that their advice succeeded because it was according to the Torah, and their blessing was accepted because the one blessed was stirred to repentance and the Lord helped him. The general principle is that the wonders that are told about the great rabbis came about incidentally, as they taught and blessed their students in the accepted manner, for success in their studies or for finding a match, without their intending to perform a wonder. Similarly, Rabbi Naḥman of Breslov said that sometimes the Lord, may He be blessed, performs wonders through halakhic decisors, in the sense of what is said (I Divrei Ha-yamim 16:12): "His wonders and the judgements of His mouth" – "that through the judgements of his mouth, ruling that it shall be so, a wonder is performed… and this is the aspect of the wonders that are told about the Geonim who lived in the generations before us" (Likutei Moharan Tinyana 41; see Siḥot Ha-Ran 17).3

notes_en.en: It seems that among the Tanna'im, fewer miracles were performed for those whom the halakha follows, because they represent the paved road by which blessing comes through the way of nature. Whereas for the Tanna'im whose opinions were less often accepted as halakha, more miracles were performed. For example Rabbi Meir, who rescued his wife's sister by a miracle (Avoda Zara 18a-b), and the halakha does not follow him when he disputes his colleagues, Rabbi Yosi or Rabbi Yehuda (Eruvin 13b; 46b). Likewise Rashbi (Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai), who was saved by a miracle from the Romans (Shabbat 33b) and merited help from Heaven in his livelihood (Berakhot 35b), and when he disputes his colleagues, Rabbi Yosi or Rabbi Yehuda, the halakha follows them (Eruvin 46b). After he was saved from the Romans by a miracle, he said: "Since a miracle occurred, I will go and repair something" (Shabbat 33b); in this he acted like the rabbis who care for the entire public, and removed the accusation over the order of creation having been changed for him, and in this his being a halakhic decisor found expression. Rashbi's son, Rabbi Elazar, was also accustomed to miracles, but his colleagues withdrew from him and did not want to attend to his burial, and a miracle was performed for him that his body did not decompose (Bava Metzia 84b). Rashbi's son-in-law, Rabbi Pinḥas ben Ya'ir, was also accustomed to miracles, and he eliminated the mice that were eating the produce because terumot and ma'asrot had not been separated from it (Yerushalmi Demai 1:3). And when he went to engage in redeeming captives, he demanded that the river split its waters (Ḥullin 7a); yet he did not understand the general considerations of Rabbi [Yehuda Ha-Nasi], who sought to permit [the observance of] Shemita because of the public's distress, and he prevented the majority required for this from being reached, and indirectly caused many to leave the Land (Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 5:5). No halakhot were stated in the name of the wonder-workers mentioned in the Mishna and the Talmud; at times they taught only moral guidance, such as the words of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa (Avot 3:9): "Whoever's fear of sin precedes his wisdom – his wisdom endures" (see Tzidkat Ha-tzaddik 210). In the generations after that as well, it seems that fewer halakhic decisors were wonder-workers, and more were rabbis who walk along the paved road of blessing through the way of nature.

sections.title_en: The Merits That Help Prayer Be Accepted
sections.body_en:
Rav Yehuda was one of the great Amora'im for whom miracles were performed in the ordinary course of their speech and prayer, without their intending to bring about a miracle. The Sages related (Ta'anit 24b) that once he saw people treating bread with disrespect, and he said: "This implies there is plenty in the world." He cast his eyes upon them with displeasure, and a famine came about. The Sages asked the scholar who attended him that the next time he took him out of the study hall, he should lead him through the exit leading to the market, so that he would see the situation. Rav Yehuda saw in the market people crowding together and waiting for a crate of dates in order to buy a few dates for themselves. He said: "This implies there is famine in the world." He was greatly distressed and intended to begin a fast. He asked his attendant to help him remove his shoes in preparation for the fast, and after he had removed only one shoe, rain began to come, and by the kindness of the Lord, on the next day a ship full of wheat had already arrived. The Sages wondered and asked (Berakhot 20a): in what merit was Rav Yehuda answered in his prayer, given that Torah study in his days was not on a particularly high level? They answered that in his days they were more devoted to the point of self-sacrifice for the sanctification of God's name and the fulfilment of the mitzvot. They further explained (Sanhedrin 106b) that he was answered in the merit of the attachment of his heart with pure intention, for "the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the heart," as it is said (I Shmuel 16:7): "But the Lord looks at the heart." From this we learn that in the merit of self-sacrifice with a pure and wholehearted heart, beyond what the law requires, prayer is answered beyond the usual (Iyun Ya'akov and Etz Yosef there; Maharal, Netiv Ahavat Hashem 2).

The Sages noted further virtues in whose merit prayer is answered. They said (Bava Metzia 85a): "Whoever teaches Torah to the son of an am ha-aretz (an unlearned person), even if the Holy One, blessed be He, issues a decree – He annuls it for his sake." For one who teaches his fellow's son Torah is considered as if he had begotten him (Sanhedrin 19b), and if he is the son of an am ha-aretz, then he has begotten him contrary to what was to be expected according to the ways of nature, and therefore his prayer too can annul decrees (Maharal; Ḥida in Mar'it Ha-ayin, Bava Metzia there). We likewise learned about Rabbi Ḥiyya that he used to travel between the villages and teach Torah to Jewish children with devotion, and in this merit his prayer was especially accepted, to the point that they said its power was like the power of the prayer of the Patriarchs. And when the Sages decreed a fast for rain, they asked that he go down before the ark with his sons, and they were answered (Bava Metzia 85b).

They further said that one who studies Torah for its own sake with diligence merits extra help from Heaven (Zohar III, Ra'aya Meheimna 216b; Nefesh Ha-ḥayim 4:18; Or Ha-ḥayim, Shemot 14:27).

The Sages further said (Kiddushin 40a): "Whoever has an opportunity for sexual transgression come his way and is saved from it, a miracle is performed for him." That is, just as he overcame his inclination contrary to nature, so at a time of need a miracle is performed for him to save him from the forces of nature.4

notes_en.en:
The Sages further said that at times miracles were performed in the merit of people who acted beyond the letter of the law and gave up their property for an important act of charity. For example, what is related in Yerushalmi Ta'anit 1:4 about a man who hired out his donkey to a woman and found her weeping. She told him that her husband had been taken to prison, and since she had no money to save him, she was about to engage in prostitution in order to redeem him, and over this she was weeping. He sold his donkey and his work tools and gave [the proceeds] to the woman so that she could redeem her husband and would not need to engage in prostitution. The Sages saw in a dream that if he went down before the ark to pray for rain, he would be answered. And so it was with a man named Pentakaka; see there.
It was further explained that about one who studies with deep understanding out of complete identification, it is said (Iyov 22:28): "You shall decree a thing and it shall be established for you, and light shall shine upon your ways"; since he has become like a partner with the Lord, his words are accepted and have influence, as explained in Nefesh Ha-ḥayim 3:12-13. The Maggid Meisharim (by Rabbi Yosef Karo, Parashat Vayetze) wrote: "The secret of the miracles performed for the Sages is that their thought is always attached to Knesset Yisrael, by their constantly meditating on Torah and the fear of Heaven without any interruption," and through this they cleave to the attribute of Bina (understanding) and draw abundance through it.
Similarly, Rav Kook wrote that by virtue of the righteous person's loving devotion to the entire Jewish people, his words have the power to decree and to influence the world (Orot Ha-kodesh p. 229; 155-156; Igrot Ha-Re'aya I 311). He further wrote that the value of one's speech and its influence is according to the measure of one's understanding of the secrets of the Torah in their entirety and the elevation of one's soul in holiness (Orot Ha-kodesh III, p. 224; 291; 296). He further wrote that according to the measure of the attachment of one's will to its root in the will of the Creator, until he has no other will, so is the power of the action of his speech (Orot Ha-kodesh III, pp. 52-53). He further wrote that one who, out of complete freedom, chooses to cleave to the Lord, his words have the great power of influence of "you shall decree a thing" (Orot Ha-kodesh IV, p. 443; Shemoneh Kevatzim 2:340). And the more he loves kindness, the closer he is to the Lord and the more power his words have (Pinkesei Ha-Re'aya 6, p. 262). The foundation for all this is in the words of the Sages (Avot 2:4): "Make His will like your will, so that He will make your will like His will; nullify your will before His will, so that He will nullify the will of others before your will."
Rabbi Tzadok wrote (Tzidkat Ha-tzaddik 72): "It is possible to perform wonders by means of the Torah, and so were all the wonders of Moshe Rabbeinu…" And likewise the wonders that Eliyahu performed. And it is possible to perform wonders by means of prayer, like the wonders of Elisha, as they said in Megilla 27a: "And what Elisha did was through prayer for mercy, and he merited a double portion of Eliyahu's [spirit], because more can be accomplished through prayer. But in any case, what is by means of Torah is greater," for it is eternal life (Shabbat 10a), and therefore the miracles that come by means of the Torah have a deeper and more long-term influence.

sections.title_en: Admorim and Tzaddikim in Recent Generations
sections.body_en:
In recent generations, following Rabbi Yisrael the Ba'al Shem Tov, who was a wondrous tzaddik, a lover of Israel without equal, wise and profound in the ways of the world and in the ideas of the Torah, the Ḥasidic movement arose. From within it there arose for Israel tzaddikim of a new kind who continued in his path. Until then, the rabbis had occupied themselves mainly with teaching Talmud and halakha, answering halakhic questions and judging cases between one person and another, whereas wonder-workers were hidden tzaddikim who did not hold public office. But the leaders of Ḥasidism were wonder-workers who dedicated their lives to guiding the public in all of life's questions, chiefly: livelihood, health, matchmaking and marital harmony. Out of a deep recognition of the holiness of Israel and of the value of faith, they found a way to draw close to faith even Jews who lived far from any Jewish community and had not merited orderly Torah study as children. The advice and blessings of the Ḥasidic leaders were very beneficial, for they contained a blessed combination of good advice, spiritual direction and an elevated spirit of seeing hidden things. They knew how to give good advice because they were familiar with the ways of this world no less than economists, psychological counsellors and folk healers. They also knew how to give spiritual direction to those who asked them, and to stir them to strengthen themselves in a mitzva or a custom as suited them, in a way that would intensify their faith and their connection to Torah and mitzvot and give them comfort and hope. In addition, many of the great Ḥasidic tzaddikim merited ru'aḥ ha-kodesh (divine inspiration), which helped them direct their advice and blessings.

As we have learned (above 17:5-8), there are many different levels in the manifestation of ru'aḥ ha-kodesh. A talent for ru'aḥ ha-kodesh is found among people of the spirit, but many rabbis do not devote effort to developing it; rather, their main aim is to understand the Torah and to guide their students according to it, for the Torah is the supreme divine revelation, above which there is none, and one who merits to understand it in depth merits a hidden manifestation of ru'aḥ ha-kodesh that blends into his thought and feeling. Even among the great rabbis who occupied themselves with the soul of the Torah, with Kabbala and with faith, many preferred to delve into the Torah itself, and their prayer was that the Lord help them understand the depth of His Torah, and they did not seek to merit ru'aḥ ha-kodesh (above 17:7). And there were some who even rejected revealing hidden things and future events concerning private individuals, since these revelations are not clean and clear like prophecy, and therefore they may mislead, as was related about the Gaon of Vilna (above 17:6).

But the Ḥasidic tzaddikim developed their spiritual talent by means of prayers, kavanot (mystical intentions) and inner listening, so that they could sense what was hidden in the hearts of those who asked them and at times even see the future that would befall them, and as a result their advice and blessings were more precisely directed and more beneficial. The profound Torah insights in the Ḥasidic study halls were also connected to their great mission: to arouse attachment to the Lord, love of every Jew, and enthusiasm in prayer and in the fulfilment of the mitzvot.

And although in the generations preceding Ḥasidism the wonder-workers tried to conceal themselves, the Ḥasidic tzaddikim who followed the path of the Ba'al Shem Tov saw the affliction of their people, which kept growing as the exile lengthened, and they displayed their wonders in order to encourage distant Jews and breathe faith into them. Therefore the Ḥasidim told many stories of wonders in praise of the tzaddikim. And as we have learned (above 18:7), in times of hardship there is a greater need for miracles and wonders. In addition, they saw the manifestations of ru'aḥ ha-kodesh as a preparation for the redemption and for the return of prophecy to Israel. Like the Ḥasidic tzaddikim in Eastern Europe, in recent generations tzaddikim arose for Israel in various countries, such as Rabbi Yisrael Abuḥatzeira, the "Baba Sali," who immigrated to the Land of Israel from Morocco.

As we have learned (above, section 3), wonder-working tzaddikim are forbidden to benefit from a miracle, for it is meant to reveal the greatness of the Lord and not to be made use of, because using it leads to negligence in a person's main work in the world, and to crises and afflictions. Admittedly, when the great tzaddikim performed wonders for innocent people, those people were permitted to benefit from the miracle, for an innocent person does not presume to think that he will merit another miracle, and therefore he does not become negligent in his work as a result. This is especially so when it is a miracle close to the way of nature, which came about through good advice (above, section 4). The problem is that the more stories of wonders were told about the great Ḥasidic leaders, the more people mistakenly relied on miracles and became negligent in serving the Lord through the ways of nature.

There were great Ḥasidic leaders who warned about this, as in Peshisḥa Ḥasidism, where they used to say: "Signs and wonders – in the land of the children of Ḥam"; in a dark place of ignorant people, wonders are needed. But the more Torah one learns, the less one needs miracles, and also the less one needs to tell about them. And the Rebbe of Kotzk said about the verse (Tehillim 106:7), "Our fathers in Egypt did not understand Your wonders": precisely because our fathers in Egypt saw Your wonders, they did not merit a reasoned faith. Therefore, Ḥasidim of understanding used to say about the stories of wonders beyond the bounds of nature: a little of them is good, and much of them is harmful (Rav Zevin). Therefore, there were great leaders of the Ḥasidic movement who performed few wonders, and emphasised that the purpose is that the masses connected to the tzaddikim be elevated under their guidance in Torah and mitzvot, until they no longer need miracles, and their strengthening in faith will come through study and prayer.5

However, there were admorim who turned to the simple public and became very famous as wonder-workers, to the point that some regarded them more highly than the great Torah scholars. Rabbi Naḥman of Breslov addressed this with a sharp parable: There was once a king who had two sons, one wise and one a fool (not that he was truly a fool, but compared with the wise one he was considered a fool). He appointed the fool to be in charge of his treasuries, whereas to the wise one he gave no authority at all; he merely sat with the king constantly. People would ask: How can it be that the fool has an important office, so that everyone comes to him to receive from the treasury, while the wise one has no office at all? The king answered them: Is it any great virtue that the one appointed over the treasuries takes what is ready and distributes it to people?! This wise one sits with me and thinks thoughts and gives new advice on how to conquer countries I did not know about at all, and from these countries my treasuries are filled. Therefore the virtue of the wise one is certainly far greater and loftier than that of the one appointed over the treasuries (based on Siḥot Ha-Ran 130). Rabbi Naḥman's Ḥasidim likewise relate that he hardly performed any wonders, and even when wonders happened through him unintentionally, he asked and prayed that they be forgotten; and his Ḥasidim said that his main wonders were in drawing the Ḥasidim close to their Father in Heaven (Siḥot Ha-Ran 187; 249).

A further problem with performing wonders: the power of genuine wonder-workers lies in the realm of the individual alone, but when they presume to deal with matters of the community, they are liable to err. For guidance of the community must be only through the wisdom of the Torah, or through the prophecy of a prophet who has been tested and found to be a true prophet (above 16:13; 17; Siḥot Ha-Re'iya [Rav Tzvi Yehuda], Emuna, pp. 197-198).

In general, one can say that the Ḥasidic movement brought great blessing in the realm of the individual's service of the Lord, and especially in the realm of feeling. But overemphasis on these created deficiencies in other areas, especially in the area of intellectual Torah study (Siḥot Ha-Re'iya [Rav Tzvi Yehuda], Emuna, p. 203).

notes_en.en: The miracle is meant to reveal faith, as explained in Sefer Ha-ikkarim 4:22. And it is meant mainly for innocent and simple people; and such were the miracles that the prophet Elisha performed, who revived the son of the Shunammite woman, and blessed the oil of the wife of one of the sons of the prophets, from which she and her sons made a living. Yet the light revealed through divine conduct in the way of nature is greater than the light revealed through wonders. Thus Rabbi Levi Yitzḥak of Berditchev wrote (Kedushat Levi, Parashat Beshalaḥ): "One who is on a great level" does not need to see miracles, "for one who has a great intellect perceives tangibly through his intellect the existence of the Creator, blessed be He." But "one who has small intellect (moḥin) needs miracles and wonders in order to believe in the Creator, blessed be He and blessed be His name, and to fear Him." Rav Zevin likewise wrote (in his introduction to Sippurei Ḥasidim, Mo'adim): "In the teaching of Ḥabad they said: Although the miracle of Purim was clothed in the way of nature through Aḥashverosh, on the contrary, from this it is understood that the root of the light and the revelation above is from very lofty levels" (Torah Or, Esther, "Yavi'u levush malkhut"), for "the miracles that are clothed in nature are from a much higher place" (there, "Ḥayav inish"; see there at length). "To listen to the voice of the Lord walking in the garden of simple life and of the natural world – this is a higher level than seeing miracles beyond nature." And he wrote similarly in the name of the Admor of Kapust, that when Yitro learned that the divine revelation is also through nature, "he was greatly moved and said: Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods" (Magen Avot, Yitro, "Darash Ulla").

sections.body_en:
It is commonly said that one who believes that all the stories of wonders told about the tzaddikim really happened is a fool, and one who does not believe that they can happen is a heretic. One who believes all the stories is a fool, because it is known that storytellers tend to exaggerate greatly in their stories, and their listeners do not check how reliable they are. At the same time, one who rejects all the stories because he does not believe that they can happen is a heretic, for indeed at times the Lord performs miracles for the righteous (as explained in section 1).

There are good storytellers who evidently embellish their stories from their imagination in order to express a moral idea, and then their listeners suffer no harm. But when the exaggeration is stated as a fact that one must believe, and is intended to strengthen faith, harm is caused, because the story creates an atmosphere that encourages a person to rely on miracles, and it undermines the value of work according to the guidance of the Torah.

Sometimes the exaggerated stories are about particular tzaddikim whom the storytellers wish to exalt above the other tzaddikim and rabbis, and this too causes harm, for they cause the stature of the other great figures of Israel to be diminished. In addition, the stories that describe a particular tzaddik as perfect, with all his blessings fulfilled, in order to encourage attachment to him, distort the faith-based worldview. "For there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin" (Kohelet 7:20), and there is also no tzaddik all of whose blessings are fulfilled, for if it were so, free choice would be nullified, both that of the tzaddik and that of those blessed by him. Indeed, the good storytellers also tell of the failures of the tzaddikim, as we have learned in the stories of the Tanakh and of the Sages.6

The most serious harm is that exaggeration in stories causes a person to lose his rational judgement, and the harm from this is terrible, for rational judgement is the most important tool a person has for choosing his path. It is worth noting that it is difficult to refute exaggerated stories, for to refute a story, a person would have to come and testify about the rabbi that he saw him throughout all the days of his life and that this story never happened with him. And who could claim that?! Therefore one must rely on reason, and reject stories that cannot be true according to the reasoning formed by Torah, wisdom and experience. For example, there was a tradition among the Jews in France that Rav Natronai Gaon came to them from Babylonia by kefitzat ha-derekh (miraculous shortening of the journey) and taught them Torah. But Rav Hai Gaon wrote in his responsum that one should not believe stories such as these. For "these and the like are idle matters… perhaps a deceiver happened upon them and said 'I am Natronai'…" (Teshuvot Ha-ge'onim Ha-ḥadashot, no. 115).

There are stories about great Torah scholars who supposedly knew science from the Torah better than all the professors, to the point that they knew how to instruct senior doctors how to operate on a brain and the like. These stories are spread with the aim of nullifying the value of scientific studies. But according to the Torah one should study the sciences, which are called "the work of creation" (see Peninei Halakha, Likutim I 1:15). And if it were indeed possible to know the sciences from the study of Torah, why did the Rambam, who was the greatest of the great, invest much time in studying the books of the physicians who preceded him, and why did he not invent, from his knowledge of the Torah, all the vaccines that were invented after him?! And if the prophets and the Tanna'im could have known physics and chemistry from the Torah, why did they not develop cannons to defend Jerusalem from the Babylonians and the Romans?! 7

notes_en.en: When admiration for a tzaddik rests on unverified stories, it is possible to create admiration for a son who inherited the position of admor even though he is mediocre in his qualities. Even when the story about the wonder is true, there is a concern that it will give rise to admiration for the wonder-worker, and people will think that his words should be given more weight than those of the other rabbis, whereas the guidance of the Torah is that "it is not in heaven." Our master Rav Kook wrote about this (Orot Yisrael 3:3): "Attachment to tzaddikim, so that the power of the reality in their souls may blend with the incomplete soul, is a very important thing in the course of the development of souls. But great care is needed, for if one errs regarding a particular tzaddik and cleaves to him with an inner, existential attachment, he will also cleave to his deficiencies, and they will sometimes act upon the one who cleaves in a much worse measure than they act upon the original person. Fortunate is Israel, who cleave to the soul of the nation, which is absolute good, to draw through it the good light of the Lord."

As an example of bad stories, one can cite a story that was spread about the Ḥazon Ish, that from Torah study he knew better than professors how to operate on a brain, and even drew the shape of the brain and instructed them how to perform the operation (brought in Ma'aseh Ish by Rav Yarov [?], vol. 1, p. 208, and quoted in many books and leaflets). This story cannot be true, for if the great figures of Israel knew this from the Torah, why did the Rambam, the Maharal and the Gra not instruct the physicians how to save the sick from diseases for which no cure was found in their time? In addition, the author of the internet book Emuna Tehora (chapter 79, notes 258, 266) wrote that he heard from Rav Natan Shulman, head of the Slabodka Yeshiva, who was one of the close disciples of the Ḥazon Ish, that he said: "I was with the Ḥazon Ish no less than others. There was a period when I even slept in his house. I never saw 'wonders' with him; he did not understand the 'brain' and did not know how a brain is operated on. In the story with the professor there was a question of values [which type of operation was preferable in terms of the risks: certain blindness or danger to life]." Similarly, Rav Steinman wrote (Ke-ayal Ta'arog, p. 329): "There was an incident with a certain great man who was not healthy, and they asked the Ḥazon Ish whether to operate or not, and he said to operate, and afterwards he died, and they came with a complaint to the Ḥazon Ish. The Ḥazon Ish said: 'I ruled according to the law, and the fact that it did not succeed does not concern me.' But he did not rule from ru'aḥ ha-kodesh; he only ruled because he held that according to the law this is what must be done, and what did not succeed, did not succeed." Likewise, Rav Ovadia Yosef instructed that his mother undergo a dangerous operation according to the doctors' advice, and the operation failed (Ba-asher Telekh, 33). And see Shevet Ha-Levi 10:13.
In the book Emuna Tehora, chapter 79, the author brings examples of stories that have no basis, whose spreaders wanted to promote a certain position (which generally distorts the values of the Torah), and out of respect I will not mention the important books that were tempted to accept them. For example, in order to nullify the influence of the philosopher Aristotle, they related that at the end of his life he accepted the Jewish faith. In Christian and later Jewish sources they related that Aristotle was swept away by his desire and behaved basely with a woman. Similarly, some wrote that the Rambam at the end of his life studied Kabbala and retracted things he had written earlier, and there is no honour to the Rambam's Torah in this story. About the Gra, too, in his old age, a rumour was spread that he had retracted his opposition to Ḥasidism, but he was still alive and wrote that he had not retracted. The story that the "ba'alei mussar" told about Baron Rothschild, that he was locked inside his vault and died of hunger, is also baseless, and was spread in order to nullify the value of wealth. Similarly, it was written in several books that an experiment was made in which a child who had not heard any language from the day of his birth was placed [in isolation], and he began to speak the Holy Tongue by himself, since it is imprinted in human nature. But Rishonim and Aḥaronim wrote that it is impossible to believe this story (Emuna Tehora 79, notes 248-252; Responsa Mayim Ḥayim, OḤ I 54).

sections.title_en: The Proper Intention in Going to Rabbis and Tzaddikim
sections.body_en:
At times a person's going to a tzaddik known for his prayers and blessings resembles those who go to idols. For just as idol worshippers believed that if they flattered the idols they would merit blessing and rescue, so he believes that if he flatters the "tzaddik" he will be saved from troubles. But instead of being saved, his afflictions will increase, because the purpose of afflictions is to stir a person to Torah and mitzvot, to repentance and good deeds. And if instead of this he tries to exempt himself with a donation to the "tzaddik" and by receiving a trivial, external "tikkun" (rectification), he will lose the opportunity to improve. And since he has not improved his ways, he will continue to err and will suffer further troubles. Therefore the Sages said that if afflictions come upon a person, he should examine his deeds to check what he needs to repair, as it is said (Eikha 3:40): "Let us search and examine our ways, and return to the Lord. If he examined and did not find [a cause], let him attribute it to neglect of Torah study, as it is said (Tehillim 94:12): Happy is the man whom You chasten, O Lord, and teach out of Your Torah" (Berakhot 5a). One who finds it hard to examine himself, or who does not know how to strengthen himself in Torah study, would do well to consult a rabbi or a friend who knows him, and thereby he will merit blessing and success in the deepest and most exalted way (see below 22:7, that it is proper to ask for a blessing for a sick person from the rabbi who taught him or from the local rabbi).

Admittedly, there are people who are far from Torah and find it hard to be stirred to repentance, to Torah and to mitzvot, and then it is good for them to go to tzaddikim, who will give them a blessing and thereby connect them to faith, and encourage them to strengthen themselves in Torah, mitzvot and good deeds. The problem is that often those who go to them are not interested in rising higher in Torah and mitzvot; all they want is to be saved from trouble and to succeed in their business. And then, even though perhaps in the merit of the blessing they will manage to be saved and to obtain what they seek, they will lose the main thing, namely the opportunity to rise higher in Torah, mitzvot and good deeds. For the purpose of the troubles and challenges in this world is to refine a person and elevate him to the World to Come. As the Sages said (Avot 4:16): "This world is like a corridor before the World to Come – prepare yourself in the corridor so that you may enter the banquet hall." The World to Come is not only in the future; it is the inner dimension of this world, for one who merits to prepare himself for the World to Come merits already in this world a life of values full of blessing. And with this the Sages blessed their students (Berakhot 17a): "May you see your world in your lifetime, may your end be for the life of the World to Come, and may your hope be for all generations." "May you see your world in your lifetime" – that already in this world you will merit a kind of World to Come, and after your passing you will merit that "your end be for the life of the World to Come." "And may your hope be for all generations" – that you will merit that your descendants will follow in your path (see Peninei Halakha Harḥavot, Yamim Nora'im 1:5:8).

Ḥasidim tell of a man who kept watch on his children's teacher and understood that he was a hidden tzaddik, one of the thirty-six tzaddikim of the generation. He urged him to teach him the language of the birds, but the tzaddik refused, saying that knowledge of hidden things may do more harm than good. But after he urged the tzaddik greatly to teach him and declared that he was ready to bear responsibility for it, he taught him the language of the birds. He heard from the birds that whoever sold a certain merchandise would profit; he bought it, sold it and profited. He heard that whoever dealt in a certain merchandise would lose; he refrained from it. Thus he was helped by the language of the birds until he became very rich. After about two years he heard from the birds that in a month he would die. He hurried in alarm to the tzaddik. The tzaddik said to him: Did I not say that it was not worthwhile for you to learn the language of the birds? Had you suffered losses from time to time like every person, the losses would have atoned for your sins and directed you to repair your deeds, and thus you could have lived many more years. But now that you did not suffer losses, your sins were not atoned and you did not improve yourself, and you have lost your life (Sippurei Ḥasidim al Mo'adim by Rav Zevin, beginning of Kohelet; see further below 24:9).

At times, those who go to rabbis to receive blessings and salvation mistakenly go to charlatans who present themselves as wonder-working tzaddikim, but in truth they are not tzaddikim; rather, they possess a mystical talent for knowing the future, just as there are people who are talented in other areas. Sometimes they deceive themselves into thinking that their mystical powers are connected to holiness, and they are unaware of their lust for control, honour and money, which is what really drives them. And sometimes they have no mystical talent at all, and they brazenly deceive the public as if they had the power to know hidden things, when in practice they obtain the "hidden" information by cunning means. They present themselves as tzaddikim, but in practice their whole aim is money and honour.8

The great Ḥasidic leaders said that at times it is very hard for the Accuser to incite all of Israel away from the service of the Lord, and then, instead of taking the trouble to mislead many people from the straight path, he gives power to a person whose inside does not match his outside, and causes it to be publicised about him that he is a tzaddik and a wonder-worker, and through this he misleads hundreds and thousands at once. Rabbi Naḥman of Breslov used to call these fake "tzaddikim" "famous men of falsehood" (Ḥayei Moharan 537). And he warned not to tell wonders about them, for one who tells their praises is as if he transgresses the prohibition (Shemot 23:13): "And make no mention of the name of other gods" (there, 212).

The problem is that it is hard to distinguish between a tzaddik and a charlatan, but one can state three rules:

The first: If the "tzaddik" says to transgress the words of the Torah, it is known that he is not a tzaddik. And all who turn to those regarded as "tzaddikim" must know that the Lord gave them a mind and a heart and the ability to choose, and if "the rabbi" tells them to commit transgressions, for example to undress and satisfy his urges, it is known that he is a sinner, and they are obligated to refuse. And they will not be able to justify themselves by saying that "the rabbi" told them to, for by telling them to transgress the words of the Torah, he has lost his authority as a rabbi, and it has become clear that he is not a tzaddik. Likewise, if he asks them to deceive on his behalf or to act violently toward his opponents, they shall not listen to him, for the commandments of the Torah obligate everyone.

The second: If the "tzaddik" cuts his disciples off from their parents, from their family members and from their friends, and controls their lives as is customary in various cults, one must flee from him. For the Torah commanded us to honour our parents and to maintain good relations with family members and friends. Likewise, a person is obligated to be responsible for his life and not to let other people, even if they are called "tzaddikim," run it. And when he enters a cult, he hands over the responsibility placed upon him to the cult leader, and becomes estranged from his own soul and from his duty in his world, and in the end he will commit grave sins.

The third: If the "tzaddik" is not a Torah scholar, it is impossible that his advice be considered advice whose source is in the Torah and in holiness. Admittedly, it is not necessary that righteous wonder-workers be great Torah scholars, but it is necessary that they be Torah scholars on a basic level. As the Sages said (Avot 2:5): "A boor cannot be fearful of sin, nor can an am ha-aretz be pious." It is of course possible that a person who is not a Torah scholar will sometimes give good advice because he has a mystical sense for seeing hidden things and future events, but there is no Torah guidance in such advice.

The best thing for every person is to be connected to rabbis who are occupied with Torah and who educate their students in Torah together with derekh eretz (proper conduct), in love of people and in doing charity and justice, and through this he will merit blessing in this world and in the World to Come. And then, if he wishes, he can also be connected to wonder-working tzaddikim whom his rabbis agree are people of high stature.

notes_en.en: Rav Shlomo Aviner, in his book Ner Be-ishon Layla, pp. 290-306, entry "Cold Reading," describes at length and illuminatingly the various methods of charlatans who pose as knowers of hidden things and future events in order to gain money and honour from those who come to consult them. These methods are sophisticated, so that even wise people who are prepared to trust the adviser will imagine that he indeed knows hidden things.
